"Eh, maybe you'll go to a fancy party one day. Or on your wedding day or something."

Phainon scoffs at that. He can't imagine himself a married man.

He gives her his gift, a small jewelry box. Cyrene makes an excited "oooh~" sound when she grabs it. He watches with rapt attention as she flicks open the lid.

It's a simple gift. A silver bracelet with three charms; a quill, an open book, and the little Mem fairy-puppy thing from the cartoon they both loved as kids. Cyrene's reaction is… subtle, maybe? Her mouth falls open a bit, lips parting, and she runs her fingers over the bracelet. Reverent.

"This… Phainon, it's expensive."

"It wasn't that expensive… I just saved up a bit from my last job."

She smiles, toothy, and takes it out of its box. Lays it in the palm of her hand for a bit as she admires it—then, gently, she brings it to her lips and kisses it. "Thank you, Phainon…" she whispers, low as a prayer, "I love it so much."

"I, um, picked the charms myself. Thought you'd like them. The Mem one was like, a limited edition collab thing."

Cyrene does not look at him, instead she seems enraptured by the bracelet. "I love it," she repeats, "I love it so much."

She slips it onto her thin wrist, keeps watch over it as the charm bobble and clink with every move. She seems as though a phantom; pale and distant, wrapped in a shroud. Despondent. Her gaze writes of sorrow; of woe.

A small tear, crystalline, lands on one of the charms; then another, and another once more. Phainon thinks her a beautiful crier, and when her hazy blue eyes meet his, they are both smiling and crying. It's as if she cannot choose, stuck in-between and crushed tight. Ribcage fractured. Teeth on the dashboard. Neck bent. Limp.

"Your sister is such a fuck-up," she sigh with a small smile; a small sob, too. Rocking side to side only a little. She tucks her hair behind her ears again. "Isn't she?"

In a fury of pink, before he can answer and say "No, of course not, you can't be a fuck-up because you're my big sister", she leaves. Goes to her room and locks the door. Refuses to come out for the rest of the day.

Phainon never asks what she's sad about. He never asks about Anna again, either.

Hanging out with Anaxa is fun because Anaxa is fucking hilarious. They don't seem to know it, though, which honestly makes them every more funny.

Today, however, nothing's funny. They've thrown up twice since Hyacine came to pick them up, and they keep claiming it's because 'they ate something wrong'—which is certified bullshit, because she knows Anaxa barely eats in the first place and when they do, they're very strict about their diet. As per their own claims, they're very sickly and they have to eat right.

So, yeah. Bullshit.

It's because they're nervous and she can tell. She can tell because she knows. She gets it, really, and of course she does—she was so nervous the night before her first endocrinologist that she didn't sleep at all. Just walked into the doctor's office like a half-living zombie.

Now, she's rubbing Anaxa's back and holding their hair while they vomit. When they're done, and my God it's a while before they're done, she helps them up and hands them their crutch. Today is a crutch day, which means shit's really fucked. Poor Anaxa.

"Anaxa," she starts, gentle, "There's nothing to be nervous about—"

"I'm not nervous."

Right. Of course, stupid Hyacine forgot that she's talking to Anaxagoras Skemma and not someone honest, like Castorice or Mydei, or Pha—nah, not Phainon. Cipher? She's honest sometimes, when she wants to be. Mental note: call Cipher later to see how rehab is going.

"No, yeah, for sure. But if you were nervous—"

"Hypothetically."

"Right. Hypothetically, just purely hypothetically, if you were nervous —hypothetically, of course— I'd like you to know that there's nothing to be nervous about. This doctor is really good, and he's suuuper trans-friendly! He helped me every step of the way of my medical transition. So, again hypothetically, there would be nothing to be worry about."

They don't seem convinced. Anaxa is just like that sometimes, and it's endearing when it's not self-sabotaging. Getting them to this point has been hard enough. It's been a several months-long endeavor, because they would say shit like "Being on estrogen seems beneficial" and when Hyacine would mention how that's like, totally in the realm of possibility, they'd just say "Hah. As if."

But hey, she's nothing if not a fucking winner. And she won this battle, goddamn it, and she's going to get Anaxa yummy girl hormones if it kills her. And it might, genuinely, kill her with how bull-headed they are sometimes.

They walk out of the bathroom and into the clinic's waiting lobby. "You know," she tells them as they both sit down, "I even got my FFS here. Did a pretty good job, no?" and she strikes a little pose, hand on her cheek, small wink. Anaxa scoffs, yet smiles.

"You were beautiful before, too. The change is subtle."

"Yeah, that's what I asked for! Just a little nip and tuck here and there."

They hum, low, and lean more into their seat. "Interesting. So it doesn't have to be a drastic change."

"No, not at all. You don't even have to get it. It's up to you."

They just nod absentmindedly. God, this is going to be a long road. Hyacine can't wait to walk it with them.

After a few moments, she hears them laugh to themselves. "What?" she elbows them, "Whatcha laughing about?"

"I'm just thinking about the shopping we're going to do," they say, grinning, "And how stupid I'll look."

"Stupid…?" Hyacine is stumped. She blinks uselessly at them. "What do you mean, stupid?"

Another bout of giggles. "I mean, ridiculous. Like an ugly woman."

Ah, this. She knows this well, too. Hyacine's gentle hand comes to grab their wrist, almost imperceptible as if to not spook them. Anaxa's not great with physical contact because they get overstimulated easily. Today, though, they seem to accept it. "I think you're a very beautiful woman—or a beautiful… thing?" This gets a laugh out of them, "And anyways, you don't have to buy anything, if you're not comfortable. We can just look."

"How'd you do it, hm?" they say, "You have a pretty unique style."

"Oh, I was terrified at first. First dress I bought was this ugly sequined thing and putting it on made me feel like a freak. Honestly, I just brute-forced my way through it. You just need to find your personal style. I always liked super frilly girly stuff, so once I found out about lolita, it was over. You know, I get pretty dysphoric at work, 'cuz I can't dress like a porcelain doll…" she trails off with a laugh, "You don't need to dress like a…" she tries to find the right words, "Like someone from the magazines. You can be creative with it or like, androgynous, y'know? You don't have to be a pageant queen."

Anaxa is extremely stylish, in a dark academia snobby classics professor way. They like tweed and cashmere and they earn enough for the finest things. They like jewelry a lot, too, all gold and rubies. They're already there, it's just a matter of getting over the damn hurdle.

They just blink and nod at her words, and at least seem like they internalized some of it. They take their wrist out of her hand, but there's no insult there. She smiles at them, and though they are not looking at her, she knows they can feel it.

Anaxa wants to be alone for their appointment, so when they're called into the doctor's office, they tell Hyacine to wait outside. She does, of course, though she would very much like to be in there with them. For them. As they disappear behind the door, Hyacine is getting pretty nervous, because they were so brave for taking this step and, honestly, she's worried that something might happen to send them running backwards.

It's not even half an hour before they're out of the office. Their face betrays nothing; Anaxa has always been hard to read, but at this point Hyacine's hands are sweating.

"Well?" she jumps up, "What? How was it?"

"Oh," Anaxa says, and hands her the prescription, "I got this gel."

She reads it over, trying very hard to contain her giddiness.

"Hey!" her eyes sparkle, "That's the same thing I'm using!"

"Ah," Anaxa smiles, "So it certainly works, then."

They wait for Aglaea's chauffeur to pick them up outside, because Anaxa said, quote, "I'm about to have a mental breakdown if I have to spend one more minute inside that hospital." Totally fair. They do seem like they're in a better mood already, and Hyacine suspects they might even be a little excited about this new development. Their death grip on their crutch has subsided to something a lot more normal. Victory! Hyacine mentally fist bumps herself.

Anaxa clears their throat, "You said you felt like a freak when you put on your first dress. Why?"

Hyacine hums as she thinks. That's a hard question. She exhales some of her smoke, pointedly away from them. "Geez, that's loaded. Hmm… I just felt like a man in a dress."

Anaxa inhales sharply at that. Hit a nerve, for sure. A deep-rooted insecurity they also probably have, spoken of plainly and loudly and casually. She was, maybe, a bit too frank with it, but it's true nonetheless. "Elaborate?"

"Ehh, internalized transphobia," she waves her hand non-nonchalantly, "Big one to unlearn. It was weird. I felt gross, but I was also very happy. I video called one of my trans friends about it, almost in tears, and the first thing she said when she picked up was 'Oh my god, Cinny, you look sooo pretty!!'" she laughs a bit, "Then she told me to stop being silly. Trying on your first dress isn't different from trying on your first hat or a new haircut or… You get what I mean. New things are scary for everyone. It's gonna take time, but it goes away eventually, and honestly—fuck, Anaxa, the euphoria you get out of it is addicting. The more I wore that dress, the happier I was. And when I started experimenting with makeup? Yeah, that hit the sweetspot."

"Worth it…" they mumble noncommittally.

"Yeah! The temporary discomfort you get is worth it. Nice things you want to do are worth it," she taps them on the shoulder to get their attention, "One of my friends once said: do it scared, but do it anyways."

"How long is it going to take?"

Hyacine smiles, endeared, fond, "I don't know. It's different for anyone. Can take a day, can take years. You just have to keep trying until you get it right. And after that, it's… really, it's the best thing ever. I've never been happier."

"Seems like a headache…"

She shrugs, "Life's a headache, isn't it? We're all just trying to make it better," she turns to them, solemn, serious, "This is going to make your headache better."

A sleek black car pulls up. The signature golden-plated license plate, spelling GLDWVR, gives away its owner. Hyacine runs up to greet her as the blacked out window rolls down. "Agy! Heeey~"

Aglaea's beautiful hair turns to her, though her eyes don't seem to find her. Garmentmaker is sitting pretty by her feet, very obedient. "Hyacinthia. Hello. How was it?"

"I'll let Anaxa tell it. Naxy, our ride's here~"

Anaxa lets out a scoff and a small groan, entirely way too overdramatic. They're committed to the tsundere bit—Hyacine can only respect it. And despite seemingly being bothered by Aglaea's presence, they still tell her about their appointment today; though, they try their best to sound as unexcited and casual about it as possible.

She takes them to this fancy boutique, claims it has "some of the finest clothes in Okhema" and if Miss Aglaea is saying it, then it's probably true. It's a respectable establishment, though obviously the clothes aren't to Hyacine's liking—by all means, however, they are exactly Anaxa's style. Neutrals and greens, with a focus on good tailoring. Wool is abundant, so is high-quality cotton. There are some silk and velvet pieces, too.

Such a velvet piece is one that Anaxa is so painfully obviously attracted to. A long forest green skirt, floor length, with ruffles. They keep looking at it, going to feel the material, then shaking their head and looking at some brown blazers. Then, like clockwork, a few minutes later, they return to the skirt. Touch it again. Then leave.

By the third time they circle back to the damn thing, Hyacine steps in. "Anaxa, found something you like?"

"No, not really."

"What about this skirt?" she gestures at it, "You've been looking at it for a while."

"I just think the material is beautiful, that's all."

"If you want to buy it, Aglaea said she'll handle the payment."

Anaxa scoffs at that, "Get it? No."

"Are you sure? You seem to really like it, Anaxa…"

Their fingers run over the fabric, almost lovingly, and then move down to feel the ruffles. They want to buy this skirt so much, but Hyacine also doesn't want to push them. "My sister had a skirt like this, once. When she was younger."

"Oh! She must've been really stylish!"

The sound of Aglaea's white cane approaching and Garmentmaker's panting perks both of them up; the two turn to see her standing behind them, radiant, smiling. Seems like she's done chatting with the boutique's owner. "What are you two talking about?"

"Ah, we were just talking about this skirt! Check it out?"

Aglaea hums and stretches out a perfect hand to touch the item. She feels the fabric thoroughly, first the velvet and then the seams. Lastly, the ruffles. "It's well-made, and…" she leans in very, very close, "The color is beautiful. Yes. It would bring out your eyes."

She takes it off the display and swings it over Anaxa's arm, unprompted. "Try it out. Let's see if it fits."

When Anaxa returns from the changing room, they are dressed in their regular clothes and slightly flushed. They simply announce that "it fits".

"You'll get it, then?" Aglaea says, a playful lilt on her tongue. She raises an eyebrow.

"I suppose, if you are paying, then why not? It is unlike me to waste your generosity."

She laughs at that, airy, light, and grabs the skirt from Anaxa's hand. As she goes to pay for it, Hyacine and Anaxa hang back, looking at her. "I wish I looked like her," they mumble to themselves, and Hyacine's so sure she wasn't meant to hear that.

"Yeah, geez. Who wouldn't?" she answers instead of shutting up.

Hyacine would've liked to look more, but she can tell Anaxa's getting overwhelmed and that they need to get out immediately. They mention in passing that their leg is bothering them, which is Anaxagorese for "I am in indescribable amounts of pain".

She stops at the pet shop to get more pigeon feed for Little Ica while Aglaea and Anaxa get into the car. On her way back, she overhears a bit of their conversation—

"I do worry, sometimes," Aglaea says with a sigh, "What if the glaucoma advances even further? It has been stagnant for some five years, but the risk is still there…"

Anaxa scoffs in their characteristic way, proud yet not unkind. "Are you looking for pity, Aglaea? You won't find it with me, if that's the case. I simply believe that you'll be able to do it, no matter what. Having such thoughts is ridiculous, coming from Miss Goldweaver no less…"

She throws her head back and laughs. "You always know what to say, Anaxagoras. Thank you."

Aglaea graciously drops both of them off to Hyacine's place before driving off into the sunset, very cool and romantic, yes. The first thing she does when she gets home is let Ica out of his huge crate. He immediately flies up and perches on Anaxa's shoulder, pecking at their earring. They're scratching under his chin with a finger when Hyacine brings them two cups of coffee, one for each.

They mellow down together for a while, with Anaxa massaging their leg at the joint of their knee. None speak, until one does.

"I feel like this thing keeps failing me," Anaxa says through gritted teeth, "Everything hurts. Everything is wrong."

"Hmm?" Hyacine hums as she takes a sip of the coffee, "What do you mean? What thing?"

"My body. It's sickly and frail. Bore me with a bad leg and gave me glaucoma to boot. And to top it all off, the damn thing's trans too. It can't do anything right."

The tone of their voice indicates something akin to a joke, but Hyacine doesn't think it's very funny—or very sincerely just a joke at that. They seem nervous, or perhaps agitated, if the tremor in their hands is anything to go by. She sets down her mug and puts a hand on their forearm.

Anaxa's experience with their own body is vastly different from hers. She's not disabled. She hasn't even had a big health scare, like, ever. But she is trans and she does get it. The frustration. The upset. The fact that she has to go through hoops for things other girls are granted at birth. Looking in the mirror, even now, at her naked reflection and picking apart every feature that she believes make her not a woman. It feels like a losing battle sometimes, but especially where Anaxa is right now, at the beginning. Sometimes it feels like it's a battle all the time.

And yet, still, it leaves her overbrimming with joy, and if she had a thousand options to choose from, she would always choose this one. This body. She did not know how sweet happiness —life— could taste like until the first time a cashier called her 'ma'am' while she had no make-up on. Or when customers over the phone would leave reviews for 'that nice girl'. She puts on three layers of petticoats to go out for groceries and when people stare, she simply tells herself that they stare for the right reasons; and she doesn't really care anymore, really. Doubt washes over her in waves, incorporeal, gone the next moment. She's safe in this body that was given to her—and she loves it too, even when it's hard.

Hyacine feels as though high on it, high on womanhood; and even when she does stares at her naked reflection in the mirror, she finds that she's satisfied more often than not.

She gives their forearm a squeeze. "Your body is doing a lot for you. I think it's okay if it needs a little help sometimes."

"Yes." Anaxa says, cocking their head, "Maybe."

They wear that skirt to work every day of next week, and Hyacine recognizes the familiar glint in their eye.

Hyacine has lost count of how many times she's had to do this with Cipher, and every time it happens is just as heartbreaking as the first time it happened. Sixteen years old and anxious, rushing to the girls' bathroom at school to find Cipher twitching on the floor, overdosing and losing consciousness.

She's not overdosing this time, thank God, and she's clear-headed enough to beg her to not bring her to a hospital. Hyacine is mad because Cipher is right, she's already gotten arrested once before for using, many years ago, and she doesn't need to be criminalized again. Not to mention all the trouble that Aglaea had to go through to scrub her record clean, all the strings she must've pulled.

The first thing Hyacine does, once she arrives at Cipher's place, is get through the sea of cats. The second thing she does is drag Cipher to the bathroom and splash her with cold water.

Cipher's mumbling apologies through it, clinging to her side, pliable and easy. She's still going at it when Hyacine lays her in bed.

"Come to bed with me," Cipher groans, "Please, don't leave, I don't feel well."

"I'm not leaving, Ciphy," Hyacine whispers to her, rubbing her shoulder, "I'm just getting you some water. And you'll drink it, okay?"

"…Okay."

Hyacine watches over Cipher as she drinks a big glass of water, slowly as to not choke. She finishes and asks for more. Poor thing, her mouth must be so dry. Her movements are sluggish, her tongue heavy in her mouth. When she returns with a new glass of water, Cipher is shivering with chills and sweating buckets, curled around herself in a fetal position. Groaning in pain.

"What hurts?"

"Everything."

"I… don't really want to give you anything for the pain, to be honest."

"I know, I don't want to take anything, I just… Ughhhn…"

"Here," Hyacine coos, trying to be soothing, "More water."

Cipher's room is a tapestry of all that she loves. One of LeBron James' signed jerseys is hung on the wall and her windowsill is covered with geodes and crystals. Posters of superhero movies, and an entire bookshelf full of all her favorite Marvel and DC comics. There are at least twenty photo frames littered around the room. Some of them are of her cats. One of them is her, twelve years old and skinny, with her elderly grandma. One of them is of her, her elderly grandma, and Aglaea, back when she worked at Cipher's grandma's tailor shop. She looks to be around her early twenties in that photo, before she lost her sight. She's crouching down next to small Cipher, arm around her shoulder, while Cipher is throwing up peace signs. Her grandma's liver spotted hands are gripping their shoulders.

There's some landscape and wildlife photos too, because Cipher's really into photography and really good at it. Exotic tropical islands with strange, colorful birds perched on fruit trees, stunning pastures and mountains littered with grazing bovines, moody gothic cities that seemed as though ripped from an Edgar Allen Poe book; all immortalized by Cipher in snapshots. All of them trips that Aglaea took her on—showing that little girl born addicted to meth all that is beautiful in the world.

Aglaea… She must be so upset right now. Not at Cipher, never at Cipher, but just at the situation. She's basically been the only constant in Cipher's life, besides Hyacine, and when her grandma died, Cipher crashed hard; drugs, alcohol, parties, unsafe sexual encounters, abusive relationships. Still, through it all, for almost twenty years of her life—Aglaea was always there to catch her every time she hit rock bottom. Always. Paid in full for all the times she was in rehab. Bought her this apartment and paid the utilities until Cipher got on her feet. She didn't let her go homeless or hungry, not even for the sake of "teaching her a lesson". Got her this job, nepo baby style. She never got mad at her when Cipher relapsed, simply held her through it and cradled her head. Took her to the best therapists that Okhema has to offer. And even when Cipher lashed out at her, stole from her, tried to break their bond, Aglaea proved that it was made of indestructible thread, strong like spider silk; and she always reached out first, never too proud, and never demanded an apology. Though she always got one, anyways.

Cipher always gets better and then she gets worse, then she gets better again. Every step of the way, Aglaea is by her side.

There must be no other person in this world that loves Cipher more than Aglaea.

Hyacine will have to call her in the morning, figure out what to do about this. Rehab is a given, and doubtless Aglaea already has a place lined up for Cipher. Somewhere peaceful and calm and beautiful, maybe a place that does animal therapy.

As though psychic, her phone lights up with a notification.

Aglaea Talked to someone.

I have a place for Cifera.

Don't worry, it's nice. She'll like it.

Will pick her up tomorrow.

While Cipher is writhing next to her in the bed, Hyacine finds the time to send a quick message back.

Hyacine

Think she'll agree?

Aglaea

Yes.

She wants to get better more than anyone else.

She's just having a hard time is all.

That's a relief. Aglaea is amazing. Cipher nuzzles closer to her side.

"Hyacine, I'm sorry…"

"I know. It's okay."

"It's—It's not okay. I've said some awful stuff. Poor Cassie, I must've… I must've made her feel so bad… You know how she is…"

Hyacine knows. Castorice's self-esteem must be kept in a very, very delicate balance. Anything that perturbs it, destroys it completely. She'll have to talk with her about it sometimes, but right now… Hyacine brushes some hair away from Cipher's face. She's pale all over, colorless, her lips dry and cracked. Covered all over in a sheen of sweat and soiling the bedsheets under her. Trembling like a leaf in the wind, like a scared child, like a little girl. Hyacine wants to wrap her in a blanket and keep her safe from the rest of the world. Keep her safe from herself.

It could be nice, just the two of them, maybe with Aglaea too. On a cabin far away in the mountains, isolated from everything else.

But it… it wouldn't help. It would only ignore the issue, not address it. She places a soft kiss on Cipher's forehead.

"I'm sure they'll understand. You have to talk to them tomorrow, okay? Explain to them. And don't be ashamed. It's okay."

"The poor boy… the Kremnoan… Fuck, what was I thinking? I was going to—gosh, it's so fucked up, Hyacine, I'm so sorry—"

"Shh," Hyacine coos, rubbing her back. She shifts them around so Cipher is laying her head on her lap. Her trembling has gone down, but she knows it's only a matter of time before things get worse again. "Mydei's a good guy. He'll understand if you tell him. He's not the type to hold a grudge."

She whines. Small and broken. "Phainon…"

"What of him?"

"I'm… I'm worried about him."

"You're always worried about him."

"He's not—" she's starting to tear up, "He's not doing well, Hyacine, and I don't know how to help him, and I want to help him because helping him makes me feel like I'm worth something."

Hyacine shushes her again. Wipes her unshed tears, looking fondly into her beautiful blue-green eyes. Cipher is too gorgeous for her own good. Her heavy eyelids that make her look perpetually bored or perpetually smug, her perfect cupid bow arching downwards and then curving up. Her chubby cheeks, her baby face. Her warm hands and the mole on her breast. Pretty, pretty like a doll, but with an edge too, something that Hyacine can bite down on.

Hyacine couldn't possibly love her more if she tried.

"Cipher, he'll be okay, he'll—"

"Who's going to take care of him? Huh? Who's gonna take care of Phainon if I'm gone?"

Hyacine takes in a deep breath, and thinks. "Mydei will."

"And who's going to take care of Mydei?"

"Castorice will."

"And of Castorice?"

"Her sister. Phainon too, maybe."

Her eyes get all big, innocent like a child's. She chews on her bottom lip anxiously—it's trembling. Her hand grabs Hyacine's. Intertwines their fingers.

"Who's going to take care of me?"

Her voice is so small, so quiet, so sincere. Hyacine laughs a bit, impossibly fond, and can't help but squeeze her cheek. "Me, silly. And Aglaea."

"And you? Who's going to take care of you?"

Hyacine's chest aches. "You," she wants to say, "Only you."

"Pfft. Anaxa, of course," she says instead.

"And of Anaxa…?"

"Well," Hyacine scoffs, "Anaxa doesn't need to be taken care of. I think they'd kill you if you implied that."

It makes Cipher laugh, weakly. She shifts to press closer to Hyacine's lap. For now, she's seemed to calm down; still, again, it is only momentary. Hyacine has to be prepared for the worst. Cipher sighs deeply against her.

"It's my ex-wife," she starts, sounding a twinge embarrassed, "I was already doing fuckin' awful, but then I see that she got married and… I don't know. I don't know why it broke me. I'm the one that fucked up anyways. I always fuck up, I always—"

Hyacine stops her there. "Stop thinking. I don't care if you always fuck up. You're my friend and I love you too much to give a shit. You're trying to be better. That's all that matters."

Cipher and her ex-wife must be one of the most spectacularly bad love stories of all time. Met at a party and got engaged a few months later. They tried to make that poor excuse of a marriage work for about… Three or so years, maybe more, maybe less, Hyacine honestly doesn't know because she'd rather forget about that entire stretch of time. Her wife was a functional alcoholic prone to outbursts, and Cipher was a functional heroin user also prone to outbursts. They crashed and burned often, but then her ex-wife got sober and started asking the same of Cipher. Started asking for kids, too.

Naturally, Cipher was left with no choice but to cheat on her with several women, and then keep lying to her face.

The divorce was really nasty. More so emotionally than in any other aspect, because it's not like Cipher had anything material to lose, but still.

She got to keep the cat, though.

Hyacine doesn't really get why her ex-wife getting married again would send Cipher spiraling, but it's also not for her to get. And she can empathize nonetheless.

Hyacine starts to cradle her hands through Cipher's hair. Now, her breathing has evened out— steadier, calmer.

"Hyacine," Cipher whispers from below, "You know I'm in love with you, right?"

She laughs at that, wild.

"Of course I do. You've told me that several times over the years. I think you know something about me too~"

Cipher scoffs. Rises up to meet her eyes. "Why did we never date?"

"You've never been well. I want you to be well before I date you."

"So…"

"If you get well this time—truly well, I mean. We can… try."

"And if it doesn't work out?"

"We'll just keep being friends."

Cipher smiles up at her, big and toothy and boyishly charming. She brings her hand to her mouth and gives it a tiny kiss.

At one point, Cipher dozes off and falls asleep—Hyacine cannot afford the same luxury. She has to keep an eye on her for now.

She looks back at the photographs in her room. Some of her cats, yes, some of her grandma. Some of Aglaea. Most of them, however, almost all of them—of Hyacine.

A photo of them as children, eight years old, playing in the park with small toy animals. Their smiles are toothless. This is a few years before her parents got arrested and she got placed with her grandma.

A photo of them, ten years old, hugging each other in the hallway of their school. Hyacine is looking at the camera, looking very elegant in her boys' uniform, and Cipher is looking at her. Cipher used to hate the skirt they made her wear at school, and Hyacine never wanted anything more than to wear that skirt.

Them as tweens in their cringy emo phase, posing like edgelords, all smudged eyeliner and skinny jeans and angst. Them at fourteen, Cipher dyeing a strand of Hyacine's hair dark purple. Them at Hyacine's humble sweet sixteen, the only person invited to the party, clapping as Hyacine blows out the candles on her birthday cake.

Them at their high-school graduation, throwing up their caps in the air, looking forward to a kinder, gentler future. Them, a bit older, pulling ugly faces at the camera. Them at one of Hyacine's college parties. Them on a random Saturday, playing on Cipher's PlayStation. Them at Halloween, dressed as Kuromi and My Melody; you can guess who was who. Them posing with Hyacine's psychology degree. Them at Cipher's wedding; Hyacine still remembers how heartbroken she was that day. Them with Aglaea at Cipher's birthday. Them bothering Anaxa at work. Them fishing. Them at cafes and movie theaters. Them at basketball games. Them on holidays, celebrating together with Aglaea. Them laughing. Them bumping noses. Them holding hands. Them holding each other.

Them, them, them.

She is drowning in them. She drowns beautifully too, loves every second of it.

On her desk, she sees a new photo, and takes it to inspect it. It's a polaroid. Her and Phainon at what seems to be the smoking area of a nightclub, faces twisted in nasty snarls, throwing up the 'rock on' sign. They're trying very hard —and failing— to look fierce in that photo. It's cute, it's a really good photo. Hyacine likes it a lot.

Cipher is snoring against her, peaceful for once. Hyacine scratches her scalp, caresses the side of her face, pets her back. Finally, she takes her hand in hers. Plays with each finger. Feels every knuckle.

She will believe in Cipher, even when Cipher won't believe in herself.

When Cipher wakes up several hours later, groaning and shivering and throwing up, wrecked both by panic and shame, Hyacine is wide awake and ready to hold her. To wash her. To feed her.

To love her, in all the ways Cipher might need.

Mydei likes his hair long, and he's quite stubborn about it too.

Part of that is because it genuinely looks good on him. The other part, like most things in his life, is because of his father.

His mother's reaction to his father, rather, in this instance—

"I just can't stand it," she slurred, a little tipsy on red wine, "I can't stand it when he grabs you by the hair."

Gorgo bought a cheap hair clipper earlier that day. It was a loud and ugly thing, and Mydei was only seven years old, and to him the contraption looked as though designed to torture him; as though it were an evil monster from the fairytales. He had beautiful hair, then, shoulder-length and strawberry blonde, curling a bit at the tips and framing his face. 'My beautiful boy,' his mom would tell him while she pet his hair, 'You're so beautiful…'

She shaved it all off that day, and it hurt—emotionally, yes, but physically too. Gorgo held him down while he screamed and thrashed and cried. Gave him something sweet to pacify him after. The buzzing of the clipper shot through his nervous system like slippery eels, setting it on fire, leaving him wound tight as a bow with pain. She kept it short, not clipped yet still ungrabbable, since.

Mydei grew his hair out after she died. Haircuts became more manageable, but never clippers.

He's standing in a small, crowded bathroom with five other men. His friends.

Hephaestion just started chemotherapy, and now they're all shaving their hair to support him. This decision was made without Mydei's knowledge, or consent—he was simply told it was so.

Leonnius runs a head through his newly —nearly— bald head. He looks handsome like this, close-cropped. They all look handsome—Hephaestion just looks small. They're looking at him now, expectantly, and Mydei sits cross-armed in the door frame. Anxious and unsure, his heartbeat picking up with all the tell-tale signs of an incoming panic attack.

Hephaestion isn't looking at him. He's looking ahead in the mirror, a bit empty-eyed, a bit melancholy. Ptolemy turns on the clippers; the sound of their whirring makes Mydei's teeth rattle and hurt. He cringes away from it.

"Come on, man," he tells him, "Your turn."

"I, uh…" Mydei tries. It's getting hard to speak. "I don't—"

'I don't' what? I don't want to support my friend through chemotherapy? I think my hair is more important than his cancer?

He should do it. He has to do it. For Hephaestion, for—he's dying. He could die. He's losing weight already. He could endure it, for Hephaestion, and then cry about it later.

Mydei hears Hephaestion chuckle, weakly, and he pushes himself off his chair. Slinks through the sea of bodies to reach him. His eyes are sunken, tired. His hair, before it was shaved, has lost all its luster. He brings his hands to Mydei's face. Touches his cheek. "It's okay, you don't have to if you don't want to."

He cringes away at that, embarrassed, because the stage 1 lung cancer patient is comforting him for some reason. "I don't want you to think I don't support you, or—"

"That's stupid," Hephaestion laughs, "This is all a bit stupid. Now we're all bald, and I still have cancer."

"I'm sorry."

He laughs again, open-mouthed and loud, and settles into a smile. Hephaestion's smiles are plenty and abundant, though they rarely reach his eyes; for Mydei, though, they are always real. He reaches up and gives him a small kiss on the tip of his nose. "Nonsense," he says, running his fingers through Mydei's hair, "Your hair is so beautiful. It would be a shame. What would a lion be without his mane?"

Mydei flushes at that, half from shame and half from the compliment. He doesn't know what to say. Isn't sure if he wants to keep speaking today at all.

"Though," Hephaestion leans in to whisper, all conspiratorial, "To make up for it, you'll have to bake me a cake on my cancer-free anniversaries. Er, assuming there are any. Deal?"

'There will be many anniversaries,' Mydei thinks as he pulls him into a hug. Tight. Doesn't ever want to let him go, as if he could protect him from all the bad cells in his body. He sighs against the crown of his hair. "Yeah," he murmurs, "Deal."

When she wakes on the first day of Rosh Hashanah, Polyxia thinks 'This is about as good a time to die as any'.

It is an auspicious time to die, or so did her mother tell her when Grandpa died on Rosh Hashanah many, many years ago, when she was very little and incredibly upset. Hashem calls to Him all those that He needs most by His side, something of that nature, though Polyxia doesn't consider herself particularly righteous.

It seems like Castorice hasn't woken up yet, because the first thing she does every morning is check on her. This mean, of course, that she has time to ponder this.

On one hand, it means God loves her very much if He were to take her now. On the other hand, it would be a logistical nightmare for Castorice. She would have to finish celebrating Rosh Hashanah before burying Polyxia, and really, it's not much of a jolly Jewish New Year celebration when your sister is super dead. Another issue is that right after Rosh Hashanah ends, Shabbat starts, and then Castorice would have to wait that out as well. So, by Polyxia's very astute calculations, it would have to be around a week or so before she can be put to rest in the ground; and really, the more she thinks of it, the less she likes the thought of her corpse being kept in a cold freezer for over five days.

So, okay, maybe not this Rosh Hashanah—but perhaps the next one? When is the next one? She ought to check and see.

Polyxia rises heavily, sleepy and groggy, to sit up in bed. She stretches her stiff arm, arches her back until it pops satisfyingly, and reaches for her phone to google "Rosh Hashanah 2026".

—Except, she doesn't do any of that. She can't. Which really fucking sucks right now because first of all, her arm is itching something fierce, and second of all, she's really really curious to see when Rosh Hashanah is next year.

Well. All she can do is wait for Castorice to wake up and bless her with a semblance of independence.

This, really, is what sucks the most about ALS, according to Polyxia. The loss of independence. The anger was the first hurdle to get over; the inherent, profound unfairness of the diagnoses. It doesn't even run in her family, not that she's aware of. She wasn't prone to stress. Her environment was just fine, nice and clean and healthy. It's just—one day she was walking, and the next she started stumbling.

The second hurdle was shame. She was so embarrassed all the time, being an adult woman and having to be taken care of. Polyxia felt like a child, and voiced such a thought to her therapist—the man only blinked and said, very casually, 'You are not a child. You're an adult disabled woman, and being taken care of as such. There is dignity in it.' Castorice's persistent love and her caretaker's commitment to treating her —speaking to her— like an adult were the only things that healed this wound. Her —Castorice's, really— friends also helped; they never treated her differently, no matter how much she degenerated. They still act the same way around her as they did back when she could walk and talk , which is nice. There is a component to this, spoken by that same therapist, that goes like this: 'You're going to die anyways, who has time for shame?'

The third hurdle was the fear of death. That one was the easiest. The doctor laid it all out for her when she got a diagnosis, and she spent around a week scream crying into her pillow before, one day, she just accepted it. It is what it is—and isn't that very Jewish of her?

The fourth hurdle is the frustration and, yeah, she's not getting over this one. Frustration over her loss of independence. It's not shame, nor is it fear, nor is it anger—she just wants to do shit, whenever she feels like it. Take now for example. She really needs to go to the fucking bathroom, but she can't—I mean, she very much can, but that would just make her damp and uncomfortable. And, furthermore, she still has complete and utter control over her bladder— and if God has bestowed such a gift upon her, who is Polyxia to not take advantage of it?

All she can do is lay there and wait for Castorice. She can't even tell what time it is except that it's morning and they're supposed to go to the synagogue today. Their new cat —well, Cipher's cat that they're fostering— walks into her room and jumps into bed. His name is Embezzlement, which is a really fucking funny name to give a cat. He walks over to her, steps on her chest, and just loafs there. Well that's just great. Now she's being crushed to death by an obese tuxedo cat.

A creak from the other room. The sound of groaning and moaning—yes, the zombie has risen! "Polyxia?" Castorice calls out, as if she could answer back. Well, she kind of can? Polyxia gives her best "Mmmph" back.

The sounds of bare feet on wooden floors, approaching fast, and then—here comes the sun, peeking into her room.

Castorice's tired face, streaked with sleep lines, her messy hair in a tight braid; there's flyaways everywhere. Polyxia loves everything about her. She's so beautiful, her perfect mirror image, her shadow—is that conceited? Maybe. Polyxia knows she's hot. She's rubbing her eyes, and when she opens them—

"EMBEZZLEMENT, NO!"

She gasps and runs over to pick the cat up from Polyxia's chest. She sighs in relief when the weight is lifted from her—it wasn't that bad, really, but it was uncomfortable and Polyxia's respiratory system is like, already failing.

Castorice grabs her from under the armpits and pulls her in a sitting position—and it is only now that she realizes how much shes aching. Holy shit, everything hurts, but especially her back and her joints. The muscles in her arms are just kind of spasming. She groans and screws her eyes shut. Grits her teeth. Castorice knows this, so she reaches for her painkillers immediately. Crushes them up and serves them to her in a spoon with a little water on it.

The taste is atrocious, but it gets the job done—relief comes almost immediately. What really sucks about ALS (other than, you know, everything else) is how you're not spared the pain. Sure, she can't move her legs or her wrists, but by god do they ache. The atrophy is bad too. She looks so skinny now.

"Do you need to go to the bathroom?" Cas asks, and Polyxia thinks 'God yeah fuck I sure do!'

She groans instead and blinks once; her signal for yes.

Little known fact about Castorice—she's lanky and thin, but she's strong. Strong enough to carry around a grown adult woman, albeit a very very light one.

Today is packed with activities, and Polyxia's already tired just from thinking about it. The synagogue service in the morning, then Tashlich in the afternoon, and then dinner at home and it's just—she just wants to sleep. She's been wanting to sleep more and more lately, and she knows why—she's gonna die. Very soon, most likely.

It's fine. She's been gearing up for this for the past year but she really, really hoped she could hit the two year minimum life expectancy; she's hovering at about a year and a half? Something like that. Too soon. She wants more time with Castorice.

Castorice struggles at the morning service, because she has to hear the shofar blow but it's also very loud and it bothers her. Every time the sound rings out, though Polyxia finds it beautiful and mighty, Cas shivers next to her and goes to try and cover her ears; though she always stops just short of it, as though unsure whether she should do it or not. Polyxia wants to tell her, 'Oh my God, Castorice, just get earplugs!' but she can't regulate her monitor's volume, so she'd just be blasting it out in the middle of prayers for one of their holiest holidays. So she just watches Castorice struggle, and she thinks it's really righteous of her sister that she pushes through the discomfort nonetheless.

It last four hours, and it's—well, it is beautiful. She likes having a community, and everyone at their shul knows her anyways so they come and chat her up; having a disability like Polyxia's is both very boring and very lonely, so she appreciates any and all conversation. Most people are nice. They ask her about her day and she doesn't really want to tell them that every day is mostly the same, so she instead she just says that "whatever she's up to is not appropriate for Rosh Hashanah"—she just means the latest Love Island drama. Castorice shows them all the new things she's been drawing; a flock of butterflies, a dragon with petals for wings, their foster cat. She does not show them her latest masterpiece, entitled "Mydei And Phainon Making Out Sloppy Style" (y'know, like the meme). She's going to give it to Phainon as a birthday present this year.

There's a new family —or at least, Polyxia thinks they're new— that joined their synagogue. A woman and her husband with two very bored looking kids. Kids are kind of her biggest enemy, because—

"Mommy, what's wrong with that girl?"

Yeah, because of that.

"Poor girl, I think she's sick. Chas v'cholile!"

Alright, damn, she's not really 'Chas v'cholile' worthy. Polyxia, it's not okay to run people over with your wheelchair during Rosh Hashanah. It's not okay to run people over with your wheelchair during Rosh Hashanah. It's not okay to—

Yeah, okay, cool, they're approaching, and Castorice is talking to a very nice young woman so it's not like they can just bolt either. She knows what follows next—she's about to be used as empathy training for some snotty-nosed kids.

Polyxia closes her eyes and prays for strength to endure this. As always, they talk to Castorice first.

"I'm sorry," the woman says, and she's trying to sound nice, "My boy has some questions about your… sister?"

Castorice blinks at them. "My sister is not a curiosity," she tells them, stern, frowning. "And if you have any questions, you can ask her. She can think and hear just fine. But I hardly think this is the time and place—"

"Why are you like this?" one of the kids turns around and asks her.

'Because I was a bad kid that asked strangers stupid questions and a God cursed me to be like this' is her first instinct, but that's an incredibly ableist thing to say and it creates a negative link between disability and badness for the kid—makes them think it's a punishment, which it's not. She has to be nice with him, because his overall opinion on all disabled people hinges on this moment. So, you know, no pressure.

Polyxia turns to her monitor. Blinks at it.

"I have a condition called amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. It means my muscles stop working." It's a gross oversimplification, but the kid's like eight and probably doesn't know what a neuron is. "Do you know Stephen Hawking? The smart man that talks about space on TV?"

God bless Stephen Hawking for giving her a more famous reference point. Who the fuck even is Lou Gehrig?

"Oh," the kid's face lights up in recognition, "I do!"

"It's just like him. It means I can't move, but I can think just fine."

"Where is the voice coming from?"

"It's coming from this monitor. I recorded my voice and I blink at the screen to make sentences."

"Cool."

"Yeah, cool."

"Does it hurt?"

"Yes."

"Are you sad?"

"Sometimes."

"Were you born like this?"

"No, one day I just started walking funny and it kept getting worse."

The kid shuffles around on his feet while holding his mom's hand. "Can you still play video games?"

"I wasn't really playing them before anyways."

"What do you do all day?"

"Same things you do, but I just need some extra help. Sometimes I draw."

"How do you draw?"

"With my eyes."

"Cool."

And that's kind of it? The kid finds something else more interesting and pulls his mom away.

The questions never really stop and neither do the stares. Most strangers talk to her —if they do at all— as if she were a child who can't understand complex sentences; they crouch down to be at eye-level and talk veryyyy slooowwwlyyyy while using simple words. Some people —grown adults— look at her like her very existence is a stain on their every day life. Like she's offensive to the eye. There's something intelligent to be said about the politics of beauty and ugliness and about who gets to exist with dignity in public; after all, some hundred years ago, being ugly was reason enough to bar disabled and poor people from being out and about. She wrote her dissertation on this back when she got her master's degree in Disability Studies, Rights and Inclusion, an entire lifetime ago, years before she even got diagnosed— she never thought the subject would ever be relevant to her.

Really, Polyxia wishes she could bark at people—thankfully, she has Castorice for that. Who sometimes quite literally barks.

It's around 2PM when they leave the synagogue, which is prime Tashlich time. There is a park next to their apartment building, something beautiful and wild, and in that park there is a lake—a small lake, nothing imposing, yet special nonetheless, hidden in a clearing and guarded by trees. Castorice buys a loaf of fresh, warm bread on their way there.

They're supposed to break pieces of the bread and throw them out into the lake—with the pieces of bread, their sins go as well. Polyxia doesn't think she has any sins, and Castorice certainly doesn't have any, but it's a nice tradition that they like to observe. Mostly because Polyxia just really likes the lake. Today, there is a family of ducks there. A mama and some six ducklings, paddling about on the water. They don't even know they're about to get a feast.

They stop just on the edge of the lake, where the water meets the muddy grass—this is gonna be terrible for her wheels. Castorice taps her on the shoulder to get her attention and when Polyxia looks at her, she quickly breaks a piece of bread and stuffs it in her mouth, then acts like she's just done something very naughty and mischievous. It makes Polyxia laugh.

She breaks another piece and throws it as far as she can into the water. The mama duck rushes towards it. She gives a piece to Polyxia, puts it between her fingers, then throws another one.

This is the first time that Polyxia is unable to throw bread on Rosh Hashanah. It's a very weird feeling, when you will your body to do something and it simply won't listen. She tries very hard, as if it were possible, and the sardonic bitch in her wonders what this means for her sins. She scoffs. Her fingers twitch weakly around the soft warm bread.

"Castorice," she says, "You know, I can't throw it."

"Oh fuck, yeah," Castorice gasps, "Sorry, I didn't realize—oh, I'm an idiot, aren't I?"

"Nonsense."

Castorice grabs her hand and unclenches her fingers. The piece of bread plops weakly into the water. Polyxia watches it sink. "I think that's enough," she says, "I think I only have one sin, after all."

"What's the sin?"

"Pulling your pigtails all the time."

Castorice laughs, says she doesn't mind the teasing. She keeps throwing bread into the water until it is halfway gone.

Polyxia just looks at her. Pretty as she is. Her best friend—for a long time, her only friend. All her other friends left after she got diagnosed. Her ex-boyfriend, too; she wanted to marry that man. Hah. Good riddance!

The sunlight filters through the trees. It casts Castorice in ripples and spots, as if she were half made of flesh and half made of Heaven. Her big brown eyes shine golden where they reflect the light. Her roots are growing in, chestnut bleeding into lilac. Polyxia thinks hers must be grown in too, then. Castorice is too kind for this world—who is going to take care of her, when she is gone?

She wants to cry. She tries her best not to cry, because if she starts crying then so will Castorice. The tears in her eyes are not for her own sake, though, let it be known that Polyxia does not pity herself anymore. She feels like crying for Castorice's sake. For her inevitable loneliness. They are twins. She is half her soul, and Polyxia can't even —doesn't even want to — imagine the pain.

"Five months," Polyxia thinks to herself, truly praying for the first time today, "Just give me five more months."

Chapter End Notes

if you enjoyed it, leave a comment!! ♡

full disclosure, my original plan for this chapter was for polyxia to die on rosh hashanah. the scene between her and castorice was going to be different too, from castorice's pov, but i decided that polyxia deserves a POV as well.

however, the more i actually wrote this fic and especially the more i read people's reaction to it, i realized that that would be entirely way too upsetting--especially for me and also for the readers. and it just doesnt feel right anymore. i didn't expect this fic to have such a big emotional impact on people (really, i didnt expect it to get read by anybody in the first place anyways). her funeral was one of the FIRST scenes i came up with and actually a lot of the fic revolves around her funeral and the fallout of it. polyxia is going to die, eventually, thats just the nature of ALS, but not during this fic, although i am toying with the idea of having an epilogue --or an entirely different work, a one shot, tied to this one-- where she dies and her funeral.

were kind of entering the homestretch for this fic. i'd say we have about 3 chapters left. maybe 2? depends. a lot of things are gonna be changed now that polyxia's funeral is out of the picture.

This one is almost 18k! Wow! These keep getting longer, my bad! I've put all of my homosexual yearning into this, and I hope you enjoy it. Also, nsfw. Phainon jerks off in the bath. Hey, we're puting the 'Eventual Smut' tag to good use, slowly but surely!

They fall into an odd sort of dance, something broken and off-rhythm. Phainon and Mydei are not dating. They are not quite just friends either.

Phainon ponders one morning, as Mydei makes him sunny side up eggs, that they might be somewhere sideways of friendship. Something softer perhaps, yet not soft enough, and still the confession hangs between them like the Sword of Damocles—held in this allegory by one of Mnestia's golden threads. They like each other. Neither makes a move.

He knows why he doesn't make a move, seeing as Phainon is unlucky enough to be privy to his own thoughts. He does not make a move because he is scared, because he keeps waiting for that aforementioned sword to drop and take his head with it. Leave him something bloody and writhing on the floor, something more lovable, something more darling.

Mydei keeps coming over to his place. After that day in the bathtub, fated as it were, Mydei slept over. It got late when Phainon's sinuses cleared up and he felt well enough to be on his own, though he would lie if he said he didn't feel amiss about letting Mydei go; thus, deviously, he concocted a plan.

"It's late," Phainon said then, stretching like a cat, "Why don't you sleep over?"

Mydei hummed as he worried over the pile of dirty dishes leftover from their dinner. His back was to him, nude, rippling with every movement of his arm. Shoulders tensing, stretching, untensing. The strong muscle connecting neck to shoulder swaying every time he turned to look and put a dish away. His tattoos danced on their canvas like women, bare, suffocating. Phainon felt very much like a kitten being dangled a thread of yarn in front of his face. "I have to go to work tomorrow," Mydei mused, half-mouthed, "Though I suppose, you are closer to the office… Hmm… Alright, sure. I'll sleep over."

Phainon tried not to sound too happy when he spoke up again, "That's great. You can take my room, I'll take Cyrene's?"

"I'm not letting you sleep in your dead sister's room. That's unhealthy."

"Yeesh, that's direct. Okay, then you take Cyrene's room."

"I'm not sleeping in your dead sister's room."

Phainon clicked his tongue, "Fine, be like that. Couch?"

"Mmm… no."

"Okay, man, then what? Do you want to sleep in my bed with me?"

Mydei turned to him like a crack of lightning, mouth stretched into a grin, flashing teeth like a lion might. Handsome and devastating. "Yes, I would like that."

Son of a bitch, Phainon thought as his knees went a bit weak, wobbly, and he was never more thankful that he was sitting.

It was a sight to behold—Mydeimos in his bed, on his side and facing him, chest naked, covers pulled only halfway, just to his hips. With his eyes, Phainon traced the curve of his waist, from the jut where it met his hip, down to the curve where it dipped and arched, and then up to the line of his ribcage. He made no point to hide his wandering eyes, hungry and blasphemous; he was tired. It had been a long day, it had been a long life. The concept of subterfuge and falsehoods exhausted him—and for what? It had all been laid down between them, naked and horrible and tender to the touch like a wound. Something that, doubtlessly, weeps and bleeds and thrashes. He blinked slowly. Mydei was too far away, and he was too beautiful that night. Vulnerable in a way, very much so, and Phainon molded him in his mind into the shape of a panting hare; he himself, the wolf. It would be redundant to say that Phainon felt ashamed, and yes, it was that kind of shame. His fingers itched with the pulses of suicide. A hole to crawl into and never come out of. An endless sleep. To drift down the river like Ophelia. His jaw ached with how much he'd been grinding it, as if he was trying to turn his teeth to dust. It was too much at once for one such as Phainon—he wanted to run. Still, he found himself tethered.

The moonlight pouring into the windows crowned Mydeimos in prismatic lights, glittering pearlescent like an angel's halo; and Phainon saw it, he really saw it, and maybe it was the psychosis, or maybe it was the hand of God Himself petting Mydei's head. He looked at Phainon, golden-eyed, cracked open and scraped raw. He had been very brave. His shoulders raised and fell with every breath, lips parted just so, and then he did something that took Phainon's breath away; he blinked. Slow and beautiful like the arid summer days in Aedes Elysiae. His hair was much like the golden wheat fields in his little village, stretching as far as the eye can see, and where the blonde bleeds into red, Phainon saw the sunsets he used to watch with Cyrene. Eyelash met cheek, and he found himself fisting the sheets, clenching his jaw tighter. A gentle movement, like everything Mydei did; the first snowflake of winter, landing like a lovely thought on the petals of a flower. Phainon was seized with such burning longing then, as though his whole chest might burst into flames, and such jealousy too, that it was an eyelash that touched Mydei's cheek and not his own lips. Phainon could hardly stand it. Yearning gripped him like a chain collar grips a bad dog, and his knuckles went white from bunching into fists. He wanted to scream. It should've been him. He wanted it to be him. Why couldn't it be him?

The desire —the need— to lean in and close whatever space was between them, mouth to unloveable mouth, was a mountain-dweller of mythos among mortal men; his shame was stronger still, and so he stayed put.

Mydei took an icepick to the silence. "Are you feeling okay?"

"Yeah, it's just—Yeah, I'm good."

He was not good. He wanted to stuff himself inside Mydei's ribcage and lick his bones clean. He wanted to know what color his blood is. He wanted to know if, when Mydei cut himself, it was the same shade as that drunken, half-formed night in the bathtub. He wanted to know what his heart looked like, wanted to measure it in his hands, see how vibrant and fat it is next to Phainon's shriveled little thing that was still beating just for the sake of beating. He wanted to compare the connective tissues of their eyeballs. He wanted to be so close to him that they were no longer just Mydei and Phainon, but something else entirely, something new, something perhaps a little crooked, but beautiful and radiant nonetheless; something melted together and sculpted into a creature that might have been the both of them, once.

It was suffocating. Delirium-inducing. Phainon has not had a sip of alcohol yet felt drunk enough to keel over and crack his head open on the floor. His mouth was dry and his tongue was heavy and there was only one thing, one thing, that could parch him.

"Mydei," his voice was far away, and yet reverberated in his chest. It was everywhere around them and nowhere at all. "Can you come a little closer?"

It ends there until he gets home later that day, of course. Phainon finds Mydei lounging on his belly with his nose buried in his Switch. Mydei holds up his Switch. "My Animal Crossing island. I just finished reorganizing it."

And that makes Phainon laugh harder. "Isn't that Raymond?" he asks, tapping at a bespectacled cat, "Didn't people start like, a black market for him? You got him in the dungeon?"

"Here is the Palace of Garbaniphoro with its seven twisting towers. There is the Grand Library of Garbaniphoro. They are preparing to initiate the Kremnos Festival."

Phainon feels impossibly fond. He presses closer to Mydei and leans his head on his shoulder. "Okay. Is there a Nikador?"

"But of course," Mydei says, and then goes looking for his Nikador, "Behold: The Savage God, The Mad King, The Sovereign of All Battles, Grand Artisan of the War Chariot, Father of Victory, Greatest of Conquerors—Nikador! The Lance of Fury!"

Mydei has put a lot of effort into his silly island. It does have the vibe of an ancient city, and all of the villagers are dressed in old Kremnoan fashion; well, as close as he can get them. There are soldiers and gladiators and people in peploi. Mydei exhumes pride, and he puts on a whole show as he's showing him around. As is to be expected, his favorite villagers are all the Jocks, but he has a soft spot for more cutsey villagers. As Mydei is talking, all Phainon can think of is reaching over and stealing his breath with a kiss. He settles for leaning more on him.

After a while, he shifts away and gets up. "Oh, Mydei, I just remembered. We ran out of bread and eggs."

"Okay."

"…Let's go buy more."

"Mmm…" Mydei hums, "Don't wanna. Picking apples."

Phainon sighs. "Dude, come on."

Mydei grunts, displeased. "Picking apples."

Phainon tries again, tries to sound threatening and authoritative. "Mydei."

"Don't wanna. Picking apples. My wallet is on the kitchen counter. There, go get it and go shopping. Leave me alone."

Phainon gives up. Some fights cannot be won, especially not when his opponent is Mydei in his Animal Crossing state. Though, he will take him up on his offer, he's not enough of a gentleman to turn down free money. He grabs Mydei's wallet and his keys and goes to the small store next to his apartment.

As he's browsing the aisles, the sheer domesticity of it hits him all at once. It's not 'I've ran out of bread' anymore; it's 'We've run out of bread'. So many weeks have passed since Mydei started staying over, and he has become a nearly permanent fixture of his household. He shops for two now, and Mydei cooks yummy meals for him every day. Even when he's not staying over, he packs him lunch for work. He bought a new toothbrush specifically to keep at Phainon's place. A few days ago, he brought over an old, ugly, raggedy Simba plushie. It's an incredibly well-loved thing, and almost as old as Mydei himself. When questioned about it, he simply shrugged and said it's his comfort item and he would like to have it here. He keeps it by his bedside when he sleeps, and sometimes he pets it when he gets agitated.

Phainon is starting to think that, perhaps, this is a more permanent arrangement they've got going on. Mydei has slowly carved himself a beautiful place in Phainon's apartment, in his life. The sun seems to shine a bit brighter these days. He's eating better, and he keeps his place clean because well, he doesn't want to embarrass himself in front of Mydei. He doesn't ask why Mydei is staying with him; Mydei doesn't talk about it, either. He's not arguing with him roommates or anything, that's clear, because they play Minecraft together every day and they're always chatting in their group chat. Phainon leans his head against one of the shelves. Mydei is staying with him just because he feels like it. Because he likes Phainon's company.

The thought is as terrifying as it is exciting—and perhaps, it's terrifying because it is exciting. Because it's a little too sweet on the tongue, and it's a little too much, and Phainon is hardly worth of it. It is treading into a dark unknown; he does not understand it, whatever it is Mydei likes about him. The Sword of Damocles dangles. He wonders if it is selfish to enjoy this moment while it lasts, before it's ripped for him.

It is selfish—and it is unfair to Mydei. Inevitable disappointment looms on the horizon. He sees it coming; Mydei does not. He should warn him of the danger, let him know, tell him to run before it catches him unawares. He will tell him, when he gets home, because Phainon has to buy bread and eggs and he can't afford to be freaking out in the middle of the store.

So, he buys bread and eggs. Pays with Mydei's card. He rehearses, in his head, what he will say to him when he gets home; something along the lines of "I like you a lot but this isn't going to work." Or maybe, "I need some space, permanently. It's not you, it's me." Something that will let him down easy and gently; a small heartbreak is better than immense disappointment, Phainon reckons, and immense disappointment is all he has to offer. It hurts like acid inside his chest. Phainon cannot bear to part with Mydei, but it is the right thing to do—either way, this sort of pain is very conceited. All me me me me.

On the way back, he stops by a pastry shop and gets them both something sweet to snack on. When he opens Mydei's wallet this time, he catches a glimpse of something glimmering in it. It piques his curiosity, and here's the thing:

On one hand, whatever it is is personal property. On the other, Phainon is a nosy bitch. The decision hangs on a scale, and it's beginning to be heavily in favour of snooping. Phainon tucks himself in an empty alleyway and double checks to make sure Mydei hasn't suddenly appeared next to him. He digs around for it and pulls it out—

A single strand of hair. Pale and silver and shining prettily. Nearly translucent in the sun. Phainon squints at it, and then he realizes—oh.

It's his. His hair that he got from—somewhere? Maybe from his pillow? Phainon stares at it, enraptured like a fool, his lips parting over a sigh and his mouth is so dry all of a sudden. It's so dry and nothing can parch it, nothing except Mydei, the sight of him, the smell of him, everything that he has and is willing to offer. Mydei, lovely as he is, that kept a strand of Phainon's hair in his wallet. He cannot help but think of Victorian jewelry, lovebirds torn apart yet kept together by locks of hair. Phainon would very much love a lock of Mydei's hair, would love to inhale the pomegranate perfume lingering on it, to rub it against his cheek, to place it on his wanting tongue and swallow it whole.

It's too much and not enough altogether. Is it a good luck charm for Mydei? Does he think of Phainon when he looks at it? Does he stroke it as one might a lover? Jealousy brews in his stomach at that thought—it should have been him. He ought to be the one stroked by Mydei, loved by him, adored by him. His decadence knows no bounds—he feels, in this moment, wrathful at everything. At the world, most of all, but at himself as well.

Phainon doesn't want much, yet here are some of his simplest desires: he desires to be the sheets Mydei sleeps on, to be the water he drinks, to be the nectar dripping down his lips when he bites into a peach, to be the clothes he wears on his skin, to be the lake he bathes in.

Phainon feels warm all over; his chest, his tense stomach, his cheeks. He puts the strand of hair back to its rightful place and decides to not speak of it to Mydei. He'll let him keep his secrets, his small shows of adoration, and Phainon will keep his as well.

He unlocks the door to his apartment. Mydei is napping on his bed, comfortable, his face illuminated by the cool autumn sun.

There's no need to disturb his peace.

Mydei also learns some new things about Phainon during their stay together.

He is having such a fit now. Phainon's been off the entire day. Agitated and anxious and trying very, very hard to hide it—failing, too, because Mydei can read him just a bit too well. After work, they were eating their dinner in silence when Phainon dropped his cutlery and simply announced: "I can't do this anymore. I want to kill myself." It simmers and boils over and wants to raze everything that stands in its path—Mydei can tell how much Phainon is holding back, and how much it pains him.

He asks Mydei to hold him, and when he does, he asks him to go away. Mydei holds him nonetheless, even while Phainon struggles. He's starting to not make sense, babbling half-formed phrases, an amalgamation of "I don't, I can't, leave, stay, please, I'm sorry, I don't know, I want to die". Mydei rubs his back through it. Phainon yells to be left alone while holding into fistfuls of Mydei's shirt so tightly that he's afraid it might be ripped apart. Towards the end, the fury is replaced with something murkier; a lazy. slow-dragging, sorrow. Woe that is found only in Shakespearean tragedies. His eyes are bloodshot red and puffy. At one point, they collapsed —Mydei cannot tell when, but now they are on the floor. Phainon is draped over his lap, Mydei is cradling his head, and so Mary held the dying Jesus. He's looking up at Mydei and choking on his tears, and there is something beautiful about him—something childlike, too, innocent and naive like a boy that does not know what to do when in pain. Mydei strokes his eyebrow.

"You have to breathe," he says low, peaceful, calming, speaking to Phainon as though he were a spooked horse, "Breathe…"

"It's horrible."

His hands are anxious to touch, and so his arms come to wrap around his waist, to pull him closer—the only way they could be closer now is if they became the same person. Merged into one being, glorious and beautiful and entirely them. This fucked up little thing they have.

Phainon glows in the moonlight, his head crowned by the moon like a silver halo. He's impossibly comely, like a fairytale prince come true. There is a stray eyelash on his cheek. Mydei picks it up and holds it up for him. "Make a wish," he says, and Phainon closes his eyes for a second. Then opens them and blows the eyelash away.

"Do you want to know what I wished for?" he asks, and Mydei scoffs at that.

"You're not supposed to tell. If you do, it won't come true anymore."

"I think it already has," Phainon whispers, "I wished for you."

He leans in closer, cradles Mydei's jaw, and lets his eyes fall closed. It takes a split second for Mydei to understand—then, panic like a drill siren, pounding in his head. He ducks and gets out a desperate "No!" before he covers Phainon's mouth with his hand.

Phainon looks at him, perplexed.

"No kissing, remember?" Mydei says, titling his head and freeing Phainon's treacherous mouth.

"Oh… Right, I'm sorry, I forgot—I'm really sorry, Mydei…"

"It's alright," Mydei smiles, tries to reassure him, "But really, no kissing. Let's just… let's take it a bit slower."

"Slower…" Phainon echoes, "I can do slower."

A blanket of silence. Comfortable and warm. Mydei's hand on Phainon's reddened cheek, stroking it with his thumb.

"Though… Can I kiss you on the cheek?"

"On the cheek?" Mydei blinks, then blushes, then chuckles, "Sure. Yes."

And so Phainon cradles his head again, tilts it up, and places a small, warm kiss on his cheek.

"Can I kiss your forehead?"

"Yes."

Butterfly wings, gentle, there on the middle of his forehead. Phainon's kind hands on his heated face.

"Can I kiss your jaw?"

"Yes."

And here it goes again, like the sweetest drug, intoxicating and filling his lungs.

"Can I kiss your nose?"

"Yes."

Phainon smells so good. His perfume tonight is citrus-y and breezy. Mydei grabs fistfuls of his shirt. His mouth tickles the bridge of his nose.

"Can I kiss your eyes?"

"Yes."

'This cannot be real,' Mydei thinks. It must be one of those dreams where everything is just a little too good to be true. Phainon smooths his eyes closed with his thumb, touches his brow, and brings his delicate lips to them. He lingers on each eye, first the left and then the right, and caresses his eyelashes with his lips. Mydei could cry. His hands find purchase on the nape of his neck, tangling along the fine, sensitive hairs there.

When he opens his eyes, he finds Phainon staring down at him. The entire starry sky is in his gaze, and his smile is shy and small. They are so close, and Mydei wonders if the world still exists outside of this, outside of them.

"I'm very fond of you, Mydei, and you're very beautiful tonight."

Mydei puts his hand over his. "I'm very fond of you, too."

Chapter End Notes
