Phainon is getting better.

He likes that. He likes the feeling of being at least a bit normal. He likes being functional. He likes being able to laugh with his entire mouth. He's surprised by how many things he likes, how the sun just seems to shine a bit brighter. He likes taking walks outside for no reason at all. He likes fresh fruit. He likes the taste of honeycakes. He likes talking to his dad, even when he rambles. Most of all, he likes being around being. Around his friends, Castorice and Hyacine and around his lover, Mydei, too. He likes making them laugh. He likes the sound of their laughter. He misses Cipher like a wound, but he enjoys listening to Hyacine and Castorice catching him up with how she's been.

He does not like looking at the little frame photo of him and Cyrene as children, but he does it, nonetheless. He looks at it everyday until, one day, the sight of it does not hurt anymore.

That he does not like.

Phainon puts down the photo back on the shelf and turns around where Mydei is playing on his Switch. Today has been one of those Grumpy Mydei days where he's not up to touching and cuddling, which is fine, but Phainon's fingers are itching in that similar, extremely suicidal way. He clenches his jaw.

"Mydei," he calls out, and Mydei does not answer him, "Mydei."

He gets like that, sometimes, it's fine, but—Mydei shifts around on the couch to lay down and bury half his face in one of the throw pillows.

"Mydei, I'm not—I don't feel well."

That gets his attention well enough, but he has that faraway look in his eyes, like he's not really here. What good timing Phainon has.

"…Why?" Mydei grumbles out, and Phainon can tell it's hard for him to sustain his attention like this.

This never gets easier. The verbalization. The shame seated deep in his stomach. Phainon shifts his weight from one leg to the other, tightening his fists then loosening them, and Mydei watches his, with tender, tired eyes.

"Is it… Cyrene?" he asks and at that, Phainon can only nod, stiff like a plank.

Mydei sighs, though not with malice—rather with a great effort as he lifts up from the couch. Heavy-boned, exhausted, he raises like a great beast out of the sea, and settles to sit on the couch. He pushes his legs together and pats his lap.

"Come to me," he tells Phainon, come to me, come to me, come to me and Phainon comes, he always comes—he is all but a simple moon orbiting around Mydeimos, tethered to his great, glorious axis.

He stands in front of him, for a moment, and Mydei looks up at him and he looks down at Mydei, and seconds pass nonetheless in the absence of Cyrene.

Then, slowly, Phainon sinks—sinks like has into depression, into psychosis, into alcohol. He sinks until his knees hit the rough carpet underneath him. Then he looks up at Mydei and Mydei looks down at him, and he opens his hands to Phainon, fingers splayed.

Phainon rests his head on his lap, feels Mydei's thighs underneath his head soft enough to be comfortable and firm enough to be stable. He feels the fine blonde hairs tickling his cheek. He bears down on Mydei like the weight of the world, like Cyrene's ghost pressed against his back, like the cross on Jesus' shoulder.

Phainon closes his eyes when Mydei's hand come to card through his hair, blunt fingernails scratching his scalp. Above him, Mydei breathes evenly.

"What's wrong?" he asks, and Phainon doesn't know how to tell him that the answer is everything. Everything is a little wrong. It's better. It is better, and he's not saying it just to convince himself. Everything is better. But it is also a little wrong.

"I don't feel…" Phainon tries, voice muffles by Mydei's shorts, "It's… I feel guilty, because… I don't know how to explain it. I looked at her picture—Cyrene's—and I feel guilty because I don't… She doesn't make me want to kill myself as bad. I don't feel as bad when I think of her, and that… That makes me really want to kill myself."

Mydei stops caressing his hair. It is enough to make Phainon crack his eyes open and look up at him. He finds Mydei staring blankly ahead at the framed picture of Cyrene, blinking slowly, half-asleep. Doubtless his tongue feels as heavy in his mouth as Phainon's does right now. His lips twitch over words, but they don't come for a long while, until finally Mydei seems to have understood what Phainon is trying to tell him.

"You want to kill yourself because you don't feel like you want to kill yourself enough? Like you don't… present an adequate amount of suicidal ideation?"

"Something like that."

"But, Phainon, isn't that… good?"

"No, it's—My sisters is dead. And I feel better."

"That's good."

"It's not—"

Mydei screws his eyes shut. Breathes out heavily.

"When will it be enough?"

Phainon stiffens where he is kneeling. He blinks. "Hm?"

"What amount of suicidal ideation will make up for Cyrene's death? When is your trial over? When will you be free? It's been almost a year since she died, God, Phainon—have you not paid the price in grief a thousand times over already? Do you have some sort of self-imposed KPI for self-flagellation?"

Phainon's mouth goes dry and he wets his cracked lips with his tongue. "No—"

"What use is it? It won't bring her back. Nothing will. And I don't think it's making her particularly happy, either. Would she want this? Is this honoring her memory? She's not even —you're not celebrating her!"

Phainon takes his head from his lap and looks up at him. In a way, he feels betrayed, and most importantly—he doesn't like the tone of Mydei's voice.

"Don't yell at me," Phainon tells him, and Mydei sighs at it.

"I'm not yelling, I'm just speaking with passion—Look, I apologize, okay…"

He stops and runs his hands down his face and, when he speaks up again, he sounds a great deal calmer. "I didn't mean to yell, or make it sound like I'm yelling," Mydei starts, "But Phainon, I—"

"You're running out of patience, is that it?" Phainon snarks.

Mydei grits his jaw. "No," he answers quickly, "And don't speak to me like that, either. I'm not running out of patience."

Then, gentle and kind, his hands cup Phainon's face and Phainon—he immediately forgets what he was mad at in the first place. He melts into the touch, going limp in Mydei's hands, his eyes falling half-lidded and then closed. He breathes out a breath he did not know he was holding.

Mydei clicks his tongue. "Oh, my boy…" he whispers, "My sad, sullen, boy…" He rubs his cheeks his thumbs, right under Phainon's eyes, where the skin deepens and purples into dark circles.

"I'm not running out of patience, Phainon," Mydei repeats, "I'm scared. I'm very, very scared for you. Whenever I'm at work and you're at home, it's the only thing I can think about. That I might come home and find you dead. And I really, really don't want to come home and find another person dead."

Phainon nuzzles into his hands. "I don't want you to feel like that."

Though he does not see it, Mydei's eyes soften as he looks down at Phainon. "Then try. Just try a little bit. Not for my sake or for yours, but—for Cyrene's. Try for her. She doesn't deserve to be a wound."

"Doesn't deserve to a be wound…" Phainon echoes. He has not considered that. "She shouldn't hurt."

"She shouldn't," Mydei reaffirms, "It's not fair to the person she was. Do you not have a… favorite memory of her? Something that makes you happy when you think of her?"

Phainon tries to remember and fails. His last months with Cyrene are mired by turmoil. She was unlike herself, back then. On the edge and nervous and full of an anger that neither of them recognized. She would blow up often and though they've always fought, it was never like that. She insulted him on purpose and, by God, Phainon was no better. They found what hurt in each other and poured salt into those open wounds.

That was unlike the both of them.

He thinks harder. Goes back further in time. Nothing stands out as particularly happy. They were never fairytale siblings. They were simply kids, with all of the hardships childhood brings.

Finally, a glint—a shard of remembrance. A night, months ago, and a ghost wearing little Cyrene's face. Her blanket, her matching pajama set, her choppy blonde bob. She crawled into bed with him then, and God, she must've only been seven or so years old—Phainon a grown man, finally the bigger brother, finally in a position to breathe love back into her. That was a fabrication born out of a chemical imbalance in his brain, but there was a time when it was real. It feels so far away, so long ago. It feels like it happened ten thousand years ago, and they were both early Homo Sapiens or even a simpler life form, prokaryotes or—simpler still, they were children.

"After our parents' divorce…" Phainon starts, feeling his throat dry, "I don't know, I was so scared for a reason. I would have nightmares every night, I really don't know why. Maybe I just missed my Dad, or… Anyways, we lived with Mom, and she worked early in the mornings, so I didn't want to wake her so I would just… wake up from my nightmares and cry as quietly as I could."

Mydei does not say anything, but he hums in approval. Caresses his ears and urges him to speak on.

"Every night, without fail, Cyrene would come to my room. I can still see it, see her cracking my door and peek inside with her chubby cheeks and her big blue eyes. She always came over with her blankie, too, and she would say something like, 'Nini, I had a nightmare, can I sleep with you?' and I remember thinking—That's silly, how can Reney have a nightmare? She's so big, she's my big sister.'" Phainon allows himself to breathe out a laugh at the memory. "I always thought she was so big and so old, but I was like, five, and she was seven. Thinking back she was… so, so little. She was just a little girl, and she would come to my room so we could sleep together whenever "she" had a nightmare. But… I think she was lying, now that I think about it. I don't think she had nightmares. I think… she knew I did and she wanted to comfort me in a way that still allowed me to feel like a big boy. That was, ah, a thing when I was a kid. I wanted to be a big boy so bad."

"That was very kind of her," Mydei says and Phainon agrees because yes, that was very kind of her and more importantly, there was not a bone in Cyrene's body that was unkind. She was made of kind stuff, like repeat text messages and thoughtful gifts and Disney princess pajamas. She was a thread pulled taut and when she snapped, she took everything good in the world with her.

'No, that's not right,' Phainon thinks as he looks up at Mydei, 'Not everything good' She left Mydei behind, and Castorice and Polyxia and Hyacine, Cipher and Aglaea and Anaxa as well, and Bartholos, yes, Bartholos too. She left her cookbook behind. And all the thoughtful gifts she gave him. She left a lot of messages and TikToks and memes too. She left her pink PC setup and all of her Hatsune Miku figurines.

She left… a hole, carved out into Phainon in the shape of Aedes Elysiae's sunsets. The hole is in his side. It pulses with warmth, but it does not burn. It pulses with life. It pulses with her

'We learn to grow around the hole,' Anaxa told him, and they said 'Our sisters are worth the pain of mourning them," too.

"I miss her," Phainon finally says, and it is a first time admission. In the wake of her passing, he has hurt himself, has bled, and has attempted suicide.

But was it for her? 'No,' Phainon thinks, 'It was for my guilt, which I will not burden Cyrene's memory with.'

This, though, he does for her. He misses her for her. Misses her for the sake of her absence. Misses her companionship, her warmth at his side, all the love she had for him and all the love he had for her. He misses loving her. He misses making her laugh. He misses braiding her hair. He misses bleaching their roots together. He misses their friendship, and he misses sleeping in the same bed as her.

He misses her and through missing her, returns personhood into who she was, not what she became—not the ghost haunting him, not the memory of guilt.

"I know," Mydei tells him, "I never knew her and I miss her, too."

"I miss her for—for the sake of missing her, does… Does that make sense?"

Understand me, he wants to say, Please understand me; isn't that so very human of him?

Mydei gives him a small smile, exhausted but kind, "Yeah, it does."

"I loved her."

"Of course."

"She was my friend. She was my sister."

"I know," he tells him again, and so uses his thumbs to smooth over the crease in his forehead, then lingers them down to his eyelids, where he closes them. The rubs them, running them over the lines of eyelashes, and something settles in Phainon's gut, heavy but comfortable.

"I don't know how to mourn her," he admits.

Mydei sighs, "I can't help you if you don't tell me what happ—"

"A bit more time. A little longer. Please."

"Okay," Mydei says, and his hands move to the back of Phainon's head, "Alright."

They sit in silence for a moment. Mydei sitting, Phainon kneeling, his head cradled in Mydei's hands. They move just when absolutely necessary, like when Phainon cranes his neck to press wet, open mouth kisses to Mydei's thigh; he does that often because it tickles him and makes him laugh. Making Mydei laugh is, indeed, an absolute necessity for Phainon. He laughs now, too, though Phainon can hear how tired he is.

The moment passes in slow comfort, lazy like molasses. Phainon is certain that Mydei has fallen asleep where he is sitting, but then he hears him speak up again.

"If Sam could carry Mister Frodo up Mount Doom, then you you can do it too and I think, in this allegory I am Sam and you are Mister Frodo, and then the ring is your sorrow, and I am willing to carry you, too—but in the grander scope of burdens and grief, you are also Sam and the grief is Mister Frodo, and the ring is, um—well, you understand, y'know—"

Phainon snorts. "Do you get all of your pep talks and emotional checkpoints from popular media? First it was Bojack Horseman, then Dune, now Lord of the Rings…"

Mydei flushes a bit, though he keeps his proud demeanor. "Well yes, I am autistic, so it is easier for me to relate to you through media, because verbalizing is—Matter of fact, Phainon, I don't need to explain myself to you. Take my pep talks or leave them, it makes no difference to me!"

"Right, yes, hmm…" Phainon trails off, and he lifts his head from Mydei's lap, stretches himself up enough to place a kiss to his bare sternum. Mydeimos is allergic to wearing shirts and prefers to breast boobily when he's at home, and it is both a blessing and a curse. A blessing because Phainon gets to witness his chest in its full, and a curse because wow, those things are bouncing up and down like crazy and he just wants to fondle them. He can't, however, because Mydei is not quite there yet, and that's alright. He is more than happy to kiss them. Oh, that reminds him, there's something he's been meaning to talk about.

"You know, I've been thinking—" Phainon starts, but Mydei cuts him off.

"There he goes, the thinker."

"Shut up. I've been thinking, uh, you know, the other night when you tried to jork my peanits —"

"Don't call it that, please."

"Just let me finish, look—If you want to start doing like, sex stuff, I've been thinking—maybe we should start small, you know? We could, uh, I don't know, look stuff up, think on it, make a list and then talk about it. About our lists, I mean."

"You really like lists…" Mydei mumbles.

"Of course I do. They keep things nice and tidy. What do you think? Do you want to try?"

Mydei closes his eyes and ruminates on it. Phainon can tell he's thinking hard, which is rare for Mydei, by the way his jaw clenches. Then, the tension eases, and he simply answers with, "Ask me again when I'm not half-asleep and disassociating."

"Okay."

"And make me something to eat. I want to take a nap."

"Okay, so… take a nap? What do you need to eat for?"

"The lion is hungry."

Alright, well, if the lion is hungry, then Phainon can only oblige. He throws some bullshit on a pita for Mydei and serves it to him on a plate, then he watches him eat in silence—the lion eats his food like there's a bigger, hungrier lion approaching. Just snarfs that whole thing down, doesn't even ask Phainon if he wants any (he doesn't, but it's about being asked).

There is another component to this decline in performance, however: Phainon simply does not want to anymore. One day, when the fog of his brain cleared up and left behind burning clarity, he thought: hold on, why the fuck am I trying so hard? Because really, why? Good performance doesn't raise his salary, it doesn't pay off his debts, it only makes him tired and burned out. Good performance does not soothe his soul or mend his hurt, it doesn't even make him happy. It doesn't even make him feel fulfilled or important or like he's good anymore. It just makes him tired. So why, really, is he trying so hard for the same company that limits his bathroom breaks to three in nine hours and makes him announce to the entire Google Teams chat that he's going to take a shit on top of it all. "You cannot change my mind. You will never change my mind. It was an accident. You both made mistakes, and… They should have announced the black ice. That, by the way, is grounds to sue."

"S-sue?"

"Yes. That was irresponsible of the city's weather station to not announce. They were supposed to. If you had known, you would have driven safer, no?"

"Maybe, but it's still not—"

Mydei squeezes his hand again. Painfully.

"You are not celebrating her," he tells him, "And that is unfair to her. She is naught but death to you, but she was—much more. You've seen, today, from her poems…"

Phainon looks to the window, and sees this year's first snowfall. A slow dance of snowflakes, lazy as if they have nothing to do but fall. They have carpeted the ground in so little time. It is white and bright outside. Beautiful. Cyrene loved to play in the snow when she was little.

"I don't know what got into her," he murmurs, "For months… She wasn't herself. She was angry and anxious all the time, like a… Like a lion in a cage pacing about. She stopped eating. Got really into counting her calories. I thought she was just trying to be healthy, but… Her shine was gone. Something… something happened. Something happened to her."

Mydei breathes out. "I've been reading her poems for a long time. Phainon, do you… think she was being abused?"

Phainon screws his eyes shut and grits his jaw. "I don't know," he admits, "Maybe. I don't know. I think… She changed when she met this girl, Anna. I have no idea where she met her. I don't know if they were dating, but… Yeah. No, she hasn't been herself since meeting her. But I don't know, I don't—"

"It sounds like she was," Mydei says, hushed, and that hurts more than anything ever did. That hurts like a knife through his chest. He cannot help the pathetic whimper that rips out of him. His sister, his Cyrene, hurt like that—he cannot bear it. This pain he cannot bear. This knowledge is too cruel.

And yet, what else could it be? The mysterious bruises. The sudden clumsiness. The constant anxiety. The anger. Hit me, she would yell, and Phainon did not know where she learned that from.

He thinks he knows now. He wants to rebuke it, say it is not real, live in the comfort of ignorance.

And yet, could he not do it? For her? Can he not face it? Is he that much of a coward?

Phainon turns his head and looks directly into the maw of the monster.

Cyrene has been abused and her life was cut awfully short.

What misery.

"My sister…" he sobs, "Reney, oh, Cyrene—poor, poor Cyrene, that is so… so awful, oh, my little girl, she was—my sister, and they hurt her, and I couldn't—I wasn't there for her, I'm such a—"

"No, Phainon," Mydei shushes him. Caresses his hair. "She spoke of you often, on her blog. You were very dear to her."

It only makes him cry harder. His hands go to wipe his eyes, and he does not hear Mydei unlocking his phone again.

He clears his throat and reads—

I am happy today because I have a little brother. He was born with teeth and gave my Mom an awfully big scare! I love the boy who is my brother, I love him because he has blue eyes like me! I love him because he is not like other boys. He does not stink or yell and he plays puppets with me. I want everybody to see the boy who is my brother! He is my brother and I love him so much.

Phainon cracks his eyes open. "That sounds like a child wrote it."

"A child did write it," Mydei points out, "She said this is her first poem, from when she was eight years old."

"Her first poe—" Phainon is so taken aback that he cannot help but laugh. He laughs, mouth open, hearty and from his gut. He laughs until his sides hurt, and then he cries some more, and he covers his face with a pillow to stifle his sobs. He is laughing and crying and laughing yet again. What a farce! What joy! The bipolarity of his life leaves him breathless. He wants to rip his skin off and become one with the earth.

"That is not, haahh, not a very good poem at all!"

"She was eight, dude," Mydei points out, "And she loved her brother very much."

He clears his throat.

I had a good day today. I went to the zoo with my brother and we fed some goats. Sometimes I feel like he is all I have in the world. I love him very much. He is my best friend and awfully handsome. And also stupid.

"That not a poem," Phainon frowns.

"Well, she didn't just use the blog for poetry. That was just one of her personal posts."

"I remember that day," Phainon sighs, "She was enamored by every animal she saw. She made me pose with each and every one of them, but she wouldn't let me take pictures of her and the animals. Hah, I remember, she—she got too close to the monkey enclosure and one of them stole her hat right off her head."

Mydei joins him in laughter. "And what else?"

"One time when she had her anger spells, she was yelling at me and pacing around the kitchen, but she—she forgot that she opened one of the cabinets and she ran right into it. Smacked her right in the forehead!"

Mydei laughs even harder. Phainon does too. His cheeks hurt. "Another one," he demands.

"When we were little, my dad bought this big sack of salt and left it in the kitchen. I saw it first, then ran to her and told her it was sugar. Told her to eat a big scoop of it before Dad gets back. She grabbed like, two fistfuls of the thing and shoved it in her mouth. When she realized it was salt, she started crying and ran to tell on me to Mom!"

"Did you get in trouble?"

"Yes, I got an earful."

Mydei chuckles and kisses him. "Tell me more,"

"One time, I was riding my bicycle outside while she was at school. I was maybe twelve. Somehow, I managed to fall in a ditch. Dude, I fell hard. I was all scrapped. I couldn't get out so I spent like, thirty minutes just yelling for help. Then, I heard her chatting with her friends and coming my way, so I started yelling 'Cyrene, Cyrene, help!' She came running to me all out of breath, saw me in the ditch, and laughed so hard she started crying. Then she and her friends started throwing mud at me!"

"Haha, what the fuck? What was wrong with her?"

Phainon hums. Comes off the high of a good laugh.

What remains is hollow.

Scraped dry and left in the sun to dry and bleach.

His sister. Abused. Somebody could have hurt her—probably did hurt her. Laid their hands on her and inflicted pain. Made her cry. Made her sour. Made her angry. Made her count her calories. They made her into something she was not, something scared and anxious, entirely lovable but hard to reach.

Right now, he finds that he cannot cry. He wades, instead, through a river of tears shed by Cyrene. How scared she must've been. How much it must've hurt. Why did she never ask for his help? He's strong. He could kill whoever hurt her. He wants to, now. He wants to see bone and blood. Did she think she didn't deserve it? Did she think what was happening to her was right?

Phainon wants to ask Mydei to break all of his teeth. He should beat him to a pulp until he is all purple and blue so that he may understand a fraction of the pain. He wants for violence. He wants catharsis. It will never come. He wants to hug her. It will never come. He wants to lay her head on his lap and stroke her hair until she falls asleep. It will never come. He wants her at home, safe and happy and well-fed. It will never come.

The pain persists. The suffering is endless. There is no place for it to go.

"I don't know what to do with it," Phainon whispers, "With this knowledge. With this… this suffering…"

"You live with it," Mydei says, "There is nothing else you can do."

"That's not fair. She didn't get a happy ending."

"…No, she didn't," Mydei sighs. He rolls off his legs to sit next to him on the bed. There is a deep understanding in his eyes. A heavy sorrow. "Sometimes, they don't. That is… the horror of this. Sometimes it is deadly," and his voice trembles. The next he speaks, it is very small, and very vulnerable, "He killed my mother. She never got to get away."

Phainon's chest cracks with it. "What do we do about it?"

"We love them," Mydei says, "We love them the best we can. We remember them. People like them, the people that hurt them, they want them to be forgotten or to be remembered as scared little things. We have to remember them as they were. We have to remember them beautiful and happy."

Mydei touches his arm. "The point of violence is to erase a person off of the face of the Earth. That is why it is poison. There is no revenge. There is no making it even. My dad is in prison and my mother is still dead. All it did was make me an orphan. And I have a lot of pain for it. I miss my mom. I miss her a lot. Her abuse made her unkind sometimes, but she was brave and beautiful and I loved her. I try to remember her like that. I try to tell people about when she took me to the water park or got me an expensive gift for my birthday. I tell people about how brave she was, how intelligent she was. She liked bunnies. She was one of those moms that decorated the kitchen like a farm and the bathroom like an aquarium," Mydei laughs, "And I love that memory of her."

Mydei sighs. "Phainon, sometimes the suffering means nothing. It is just suffering. And it is not grand."

"That's… awful."

"It is. It's awful," he rubs some tears from Phainon's cheek away, "So do not let it define her. She was not awful. You have to tell people about how amazing she was. You cannot let her be suffering. She cannot be a wound."

"I wish I had more time. I wish I could have helped her. I wish I could have told her I loved her more. I wish we didn't get into that fight. That was a stupid fight."

"Siblings fight. Even I know that and I'm an only child. If there wasn't an accident, you would've slept it off and been best friends in the morning again."

"Ha! Yeah, probably…"

"Your guilt is awfully self-centered. It should not be about you. It should be about her. And I think she would prefer that her brother, who was born with teeth, be a little kinder both to himself and to her," Mydei boops his nose, "You have suffered enough. If you need to hear it, then here—it was an accident, and I absolve you."

Born with teeth. He wants to bite a chunk out of the world, dig it into the dirt and pull Cyrene from her grave, devour her, absorb her into himself, so she might live again. So she might take his body and do better things with it than he ever could. So he can watch from whatever void is waiting for him and smile and nod and know it was the right choice. Instead, he feels some raspy, hollow noise crumple in his throat.

Mydei holds him until he learns how to cry.

'It would be better if she was here. I wish she was here. I wish she didn't die,' he repeats in warbling tones, off-key, waterlogged. All hideously juvenile statements, but he says them anyway, feels like a boy anyways—clinging to his stuffie, climbing into his big sister's bed, asking her to teach him how to be brave with all the monsters in the world. That he got bigger and broader and, one day, older than her means nothing. That is still his big sister. He is still that little boy, grown tall.

At some point, the crying exhausts him to the point of sleep. Mydei messages Tribios and takes a day off—unpaid, goddamn it—for Phainon.

The next morning, the pain is still there. Hollow and dull, but it exists nonetheless. It must be as Anaxa said. It never goes away. There is a hole and he must grow around it.

He decides that there is no option but to grow. Cutting it at the root kills the last person that knew Cyrene as she was; smiling, mischievous, cheeky at times, intelligent, sensitive, and awfully funny. He checks in with his debt collector. He's still got at least two more years to pay for her funeral. It's no matter. It's a small price to pay for giving Cyrene a beautiful send-off; though, Phainon suspects, she would've much more preferred something more intimate. Sorry, Cyrene. That is simply what he thought was most fitting in the moment.

It feels less heavy, in a way. Not in any particularly comfortable way, but, as Anaxa said, our sisters are worth the pain of mourning them.

There is no revenge. Her abuser is anonymous. They have tried to wipe the memory of her clean, as if she never existed. Instead, she left ripples behind, small and weak but indisputably there. Phainon finds the reflection of his younger self in those ripples. She is next to him. He carries this as he carried her coffin; nobly, with dignity, and sober grief. She is worth it. She has always been worth it.

Her poetry blog… What a beautiful legacy. He calls Castorice and asks if she can bind a book for him like she does her fan fictions.

"Of course I can!" she says, her face a little too close to the camera, "I can even get Polyxia to draw a cover for it! Would you like that?"

"Yes, I would."

"What do you want the cover to be?"

"Hmm… A quill on an open book. And one of those Mems from that one fairy cartoon, you know the one?"

"Oh, yeah, totally, I do! Did'ya hear that, Polyxia?"

"I did. You want a book on a book cover? I mean, sure, whatever floats your boat. I'll do it for a cigarette."

"Polyxia, NO! Phainon, sorry, I have to go—message me what you want bound!"

The video call cuts off and Phainon chuckles fondly. He hears Mydei snore in the bedroom.

Phainon takes a sip of his coffee and, as he walks around the living room, he stops to look at the framed picture of Cyrene he holds on a shelf. He grabs it and brings it closer.

This photo is three years old. She's wearing a white summer dress, spaghetti straps and all, and her olive skin has been kissed by the sun. Their first and only beach vacation. Phainon took that picture. She is holding a cocktail in her hand, fancy glass and swirly straw and orange slice, and she is smiling ear to ear. Her gaze is not at the camera, but rather to the side. Phainon captured her well. The freckles on her shoulders, the dimples they both have, the crow's feet in the corner of her eyes which only showed up when she smiled. The wrinkle in her straight nose, her acne scars, her bushy eyebrows. Her hold on the glass is delicate but firm, and she seems to be half-heartedly playing with the straw. It is an incredible candid. Her blue eyes glitter with all the streetlights, a million little pinpricks of light as though the starry night sky above itself was reflected in them.

Phainon loves this picture of her. He looks at it for a long time.

For the first time ever, this unmoving still, this slice of a life shortly lived, seems to be looking back—and in her eyes, now alive, there is a clever, impish glint.
